reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents a purported free-BNB flash-loan arbitrage opportunity with deployment instructions and a claimed unusually large return. The opportunity is tied to sending more BNB, while the demonstrated contract and wallet flow show payable interaction, a BNB recipient transfer, and transaction confirmation. The final recipient, transaction outcome, and whether funds were recovered are not established.

citations.quote: AMAZING!! "NO CODE" FREE FLASH LOANS ARBITRAGE BOT.
Flash loan arbitrage tutorial to get FREE BNB with no collateral using a BNB flash loan attack
Step 7: Connect your wallet when prompted (Metamask Preferable)
Step 8: Enter your token details and deploy the contract (MyToken)
Step 17: Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps

opening.argument: Judge, the description does more than celebrate an opportunity: it warns that flash-loan exploits have been used to attack vulnerable protocols and steal money. It also poses the question of what to think about crypto flash loans and invites viewers to watch a review. Those words support reading the video as an examination of a risky technique, not an unqualified endorsement. The instructions may be imprudent, but the warning matters when assessing the creator's purpose.

citations.quote: flash loan exploits have been used to attack vulnerable DeFi protocols and steal millions of dollars.
What do I think about such crypto flash loans and are Binance loans better? - Watch this Binance loans review until the end to find out.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening cites the promise of free BNB and the instruction to send BNB, but neither quotation alone proves what happens to the funds. The description characterizes the transfer as covering swaps and gives a fee estimate. That explanation deserves scrutiny; it should not be silently replaced with a demonstrated loss. The warning about exploits also complicates a reading of the entire video as simple, risk-free solicitation.

citations.quote: Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
it's going to take around 0.18-0.19 BNB fees
flash loan exploits have been used to attack vulnerable DeFi protocols and steal millions of dollars.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The exploit warning concerns attacks on DeFi protocols; it does not warn viewers that following these instructions could cost them their BNB. The same description tells viewers to send at least 0.2 BNB to a contract, then try sending more if it does not work. The narration directly links paying more to getting more. No demonstrated loss is needed to recognize that the video promotes a funded contract as a route to returns.

citations.quote: Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
if it doesn't work with 0.2 BNB try to send another 0.2 BNB
The more BNB you send the more you get.

opening.argument: Judge, much of the supplied material is a procedural smart-contract demonstration: create a Solidity file, compile it, connect a wallet, deploy, and call a function. The sampled frames show a compiler, contract code, and a wallet confirmation interface. Those details support treating the video as a technology walkthrough. Even the narrator's claimed result is presented as personal experience, not independent proof that every viewer will obtain it. A questionable demonstration should be judged on what it actually shows, rather than assuming an unseen outcome.

citations.quote: Step 2: Click the contracts folder then the create new file icon, create a file call it contract.sol hit ENTER
Step 4: Click compile contract.sol
I got more than $3.8 billion in one flash loan

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies a funding instruction, but deployment and wallet interaction are also the subject of the walkthrough. The cited steps do not establish the recipient's ultimate control of the funds or a completed loss. The visible wallet confirmation is consistent with the narrator demonstrating a contract interaction; its presence cannot, by itself, settle whether the tutorial is deceptive.

citations.quote: Step 8: Enter your token details and deploy the contract (MyToken)
Step 19: Call “action” function.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The software steps are real features of the presentation, but they lead viewers to fund the deployed contract. The description instructs a BNB transfer before calling “action,” and the narration says a larger payment produces a larger return. The enormous claimed result reinforces that pitch. Calling the sequence a walkthrough does not explain away its request for funds or its asserted payoff.

citations.quote: Step 17: Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
Step 19: Call “action” function.
You can get more if you pay more fees.
I got more than $3.8 billion in one flash loan

opening.argument: Judge, the specified BNB payment is described as a charge for performing swaps, with an estimated range and a warning that fees vary. On that account, the payment is an operating cost of the proposed contract activity, not expressly a purchase of a guaranteed payout. The quoted instructions do not show a request for a password or recovery phrase, a recruitment requirement, or a verified loss. The distinction is narrow but important: an implausible financial claim does not, without more, establish where a viewer's transfer ultimately goes.

citations.quote: Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
it's going to take around 0.18-0.19 BNB fees
because fees may be different from day to day.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats the transfer as evidence of a funded-return scheme, yet its own cited step calls the BNB a swap gas fee. The cited title and free-BNB language are promotional claims, not proof of the contract's operation or the recipient's identity. The supplied account supports concern, but it does not establish a completed diversion of funds or show what the contract ultimately delivered.

citations.quote: Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
AMAZING!! "NO CODE" FREE FLASH LOANS ARBITRAGE BOT.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the transfer a fee does not make it an ordinary service charge. Viewers are told to send BNB to a newly generated contract address, send more if the first amount does not work, and expect more when they pay more. That is a funding instruction tied to a promised return. The absence of a visible recovery phrase or proven loss does not remove the mechanism shown in the video's own instructions.
